claim: The complex of methyltransferase-like proteins 3 and 14 (METTL3-14) is the major enzyme that deposits N6-methyladenosine (m6A) modifications on messenger RNA (mRNA) in humans.
source: The complex of methyltransferase-like proteins 3 and 14 (METTL3-14) is the major enzyme that deposits N6-methyladenosine (m6A) modifications on messenger RNA (mRNA) in humans.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in the field, supported by the citation to Liu et al., 2014 in the introduction section.

claim: METTL3-14 plays key roles in various biological processes through its methyltransferase (MTase) activity.
source: METTL3-14 plays key roles in various biological processes through its methyltransferase (MTase) activity.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations in the introduction discussing various biological roles.

claim: Molecular dynamics simulations based on crystal structures of METTL3-14 with BAs suggest that the Y406 side chain of METTL3 is involved in the recruitment of adenosine and release of m6A.
source: Molecular dynamics simulations based on crystal structures of METTL3-14 with BAs suggest that the Y406 side chain of METTL3 is involved in the recruitment of adenosine and release of m6A.
evidence: This claim is supported by MD simulation data presented in the manuscript, particularly in Figure 5 and related text.

claim: A crystal structure with a BA representing the transition state of methyl transfer shows a direct involvement of the METTL3 side chains E481 and K513 in adenosine binding.
source: A crystal structure with a BA representing the transition state of methyl transfer shows a direct involvement of the METTL3 side chains E481 and K513 in adenosine binding which is supported by mutational analysis.
evidence: This is supported by the crystal structure data shown in Figure 3 and Figure 4, and mutational analysis in Figure 4C.

claim: Quantum mechanics/molecular mechanics (QM/MM) free energy calculations indicate that methyl transfer occurs without prior deprotonation of adenosine-N6.
source: Quantum mechanics/molecular mechanics (QM/MM) free energy calculations indicate that methyl transfer occurs without prior deprotonation of adenosine-N6.
evidence: This is supported by QM/MM calculations presented in Figure 8 and Table 3.

claim: The QM/MM calculations provide further support for the role of electrostatic contributions of E481 and K513 to catalysis.
source: Furthermore, the QM/MM calculations provide further support for the role of electrostatic contributions of E481 and K513 to catalysis.
evidence: This is supported by the QM/MM simulation results and structural analysis in Figure 8.

claim: The product release step is rate-limiting for METTL3.
source: Taken together, the QM/MM and MD simulations suggest that the dissociation of the coproduct SAH and product RNA is likely the rate-limiting step.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing the QM/MM barrier height (~15-16 kcal/mol) with the experimental turnover rate (0.2-0.6 min-1, ~20 kcal/mol barrier).

claim: N6-methyladenosine (m6A) is the most frequent internal modification of messenger RNA (mRNA) within the consensus sequence GGACU.
source: N6-methyladenosine (m6A) is the most frequent internal modification of messenger RNA (mRNA) within the consensus sequence GGACU that is enriched near stop codons and in 3' untranslated regions (Roundtree et al., 2017; Fu et al., 2014; Linder et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Roundtree et al., 2017; Fu et al., 2014; Linder et al., 2015.

claim: m6A is enriched near stop codons and in 3' untranslated regions.
source: N6-methyladenosine (m6A) is the most frequent internal modification of messenger RNA (mRNA) within the consensus sequence GGACU that is enriched near stop codons and in 3' untranslated regions (Roundtree et al., 2017; Fu et al., 2014; Linder et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Roundtree et al., 2017; Fu et al., 2014; Linder et al., 2015.

claim: m6A affects alternative polyadenylation.
source: m6A affects most aspects of RNA regulation, i.e., alternative polyadenylation (Ke et al., 2015), splicing (Ke et al., 2017), nuclear export (Lesbirel and Wilson, 2019), stability (Lee et al., 2020), and translation initiation (Fu et al., 2014; Kadumuri and Janga, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ke et al., 2015.

claim: m6A affects splicing.
source: m6A affects most aspects of RNA regulation, i.e., alternative polyadenylation (Ke et al., 2015), splicing (Ke et al., 2017), nuclear export (Lesbirel and Wilson, 2019), stability (Lee et al., 2020), and translation initiation (Fu et al., 2014; Kadumuri and Janga, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ke et al., 2017.

claim: m6A affects nuclear export.
source: m6A affects most aspects of RNA regulation, i.e., alternative polyadenylation (Ke et al., 2015), splicing (Ke et al., 2017), nuclear export (Lesbirel and Wilson, 2019), stability (Lee et al., 2020), and translation initiation (Fu et al., 2014; Kadumuri and Janga, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lesbirel and Wilson, 2019.

claim: m6A affects RNA stability.
source: m6A affects most aspects of RNA regulation, i.e., alternative polyadenylation (Ke et al., 2015), splicing (Ke et al., 2017), nuclear export (Lesbirel and Wilson, 2019), stability (Lee et al., 2020), and translation initiation (Fu et al., 2014; Kadumuri and Janga, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lee et al., 2020.

claim: m6A affects translation initiation.
source: m6A affects most aspects of RNA regulation, i.e., alternative polyadenylation (Ke et al., 2015), splicing (Ke et al., 2017), nuclear export (Lesbirel and Wilson, 2019), stability (Lee et al., 2020), and translation initiation (Fu et al., 2014; Kadumuri and Janga, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Fu et al., 2014; Kadumuri and Janga, 2018.

claim: The METTL3-14 heterodimer is involved in type 2 diabetes.
source: The METTL3-14 heterodimer is involved in a wide variety of diseases including type 2 diabetes (De Jesus et al., 2019), viral infections (Dang et al., 2019), and several types of cancer (Chen et al., 2019b).
evidence: This is supported by citation to De Jesus et al., 2019.

claim: The METTL3-14 heterodimer is involved in viral infections.
source: The METTL3-14 heterodimer is involved in a wide variety of diseases including type 2 diabetes (De Jesus et al., 2019), viral infections (Dang et al., 2019), and several types of cancer (Chen et al., 2019b).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Dang et al., 2019.

claim: The METTL3-14 heterodimer is involved in several types of cancer.
source: The METTL3-14 heterodimer is involved in a wide variety of diseases including type 2 diabetes (De Jesus et al., 2019), viral infections (Dang et al., 2019), and several types of cancer (Chen et al., 2019b).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Chen et al., 2019b.

claim: METTL3-mediated m6A deposition is directly involved in the development of acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) by promoting the translation of genes involved in cell growth, differentiation, and apoptosis.
source: METTL3-mediated m6A deposition is directly involved in the development of acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) by promoting the translation of genes involved in cell growth, differentiation, and apoptosis (Barbieri et al., 2017; Vu et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Barbieri et al., 2017; Vu et al., 2017.

claim: Inhibition of the METTL3 catalytic function is sufficient to induce apoptosis and differentiation in AML cells and in a mouse model of the disease but not in normal non-leukaemic haematopoietic cells.
source: It has been demonstrated that inhibition of the METTL3 catalytic function is sufficient to induce apoptosis and differentiation in AML cells and in a mouse model of the disease but not in normal non-leukaemic haematopoietic cells (Moroz-Omori et al., 2021; Yankova et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Moroz-Omori et al., 2021; Yankova et al., 2021.

claim: The role of METTL3-14 varies in different cancer types, acting as oncogene or tumour suppressor.
source: While it has been well established that METTL3-14 dysregulation is related to cancer development, the role of METTL3-14 varies in different cancer types, i.e., it can act as oncogene or tumour suppressor (Zeng et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Zeng et al., 2020.

claim: METTL3-14 transfers the methyl group from S-adenosylmethionine (SAM) to the substrate adenosine.
source: METTL3-14 is the catalytic complex that transfers the methyl group from S-adenosylmethionine (SAM) to the substrate adenosine (Figure 1; Wang et al., 2016b; Wang et al., 2016a; Śledź and Jinek, 2016; Yoshida et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: METTL3 comprises a low-complexity region at the N-terminus, a zinc finger responsible for substrate binding, and the catalytic MTase domain at the C-terminus.
source: METTL3 comprises a low-complexity region at the N-terminus, a zinc finger responsible for substrate binding, and the catalytic MTase domain at the C-terminus (Figure 1A; Huang et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Huang et al., 2019 and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The METTL3 MTase domain has the catalytically active SAM binding site and adopts a Rossmann fold that is characteristic of Class I SAM-dependent MTases.
source: The METTL3 MTase domain has the catalytically active SAM binding site and adopts a Rossmann fold that is characteristic of Class I SAM-dependent MTases (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is based on structural knowledge and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: METTL14 has an MTase domain with a redundant active site of hitherto unknown function.
source: METTL14 has an MTase domain, too, however, with a redundant active site of hitherto unknown function, and so-called RGG repeats at its C-terminus essential for RNA binding (Yoshida et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Yoshida et al., 2022.

claim: METTL14 has RGG repeats at its C-terminus essential for RNA binding.
source: METTL14 has an MTase domain, too, however, with a redundant active site of hitherto unknown function, and so-called RGG repeats at its C-terminus essential for RNA binding (Yoshida et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Yoshida et al., 2022.

claim: METTL14 plays a structural role for complex stabilisation and RNA binding.
source: METTL14 plays a structural role for complex stabilisation and RNA binding.
evidence: This is based on structural and functional studies cited in the manuscript.

claim: METTL14 forms a positively charged groove at the interface with METTL3 which is predicted to be the RNA binding site.
source: It forms a positively charged groove at the interface with METTL3 which is predicted to be the RNA binding site.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1B and based on structural analysis.

claim: BA2 has an IC50 of 9±1 µM for METTL3-14.
evidence: This is measured experimentally using the TR-FRET assay as shown in Table 1 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: BA4 has an IC50 of 18±3 µM for METTL3-14.
evidence: This is measured experimentally using the TR-FRET assay as shown in Table 1 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: All the crystallised BAs bind in the METTL3 active site.
source: All the crystallised BAs bind in the METTL3 active site (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is shown in the crystal structures presented in Figure 3A.

claim: For BA2 and BA4, the interaction of their SAM-like moiety is the same as for SAM.
source: For BA2 and BA4, however, the interaction of their SAM-like moiety is the same as for SAM (Figure 3B–F and Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown in the crystal structures and interaction diagrams in Figure 3.

claim: BA2 and BA4 bind with their SAM moiety in the active site lined with METTL3 hydrophobic residues and form polar contacts to conserved residues D395, R536, H538, and N539 via the methionine part.
source: Both ligands bind with their SAM moiety in the active site lined with METTL3 hydrophobic residues and form polar contacts to conserved residues, namely D395, R536, H538, and N539 via the methionine part and D377, I378, F534, N549, and Q550 via the adenosine moiety of 5'N-SAM.
evidence: This is shown in the crystal structures in Figure 3.

claim: BA2 and BA4 form polar contacts to conserved residues D377, I378, F534, N549, and Q550 via the adenosine moiety of 5'N-SAM.
source: Both ligands bind with their SAM moiety in the active site lined with METTL3 hydrophobic residues and form polar contacts to conserved residues, namely D395, R536, H538, and N539 via the methionine part and D377, I378, F534, N549, and Q550 via the adenosine moiety of 5'N-SAM.
evidence: This is shown in the crystal structures in Figure 3.

claim: The classical m6A MTase catalytic 395DPPW398 motif of METTL3 in its flexible active site loop 1 (ASL1, METTL3 residues 395–410) participates to the binding of adenosine.
source: The classical m6A MTase catalytic 395DPPW398 motif (D/N-PP-Y/F/W) of METTL3 in its flexible active site loop 1 (ASL1, METTL3 residues 395–410) participates to the binding of adenosine.
evidence: This is shown in the crystal structures and supported by mutational analysis.

claim: D395 forms a salt bridge to SAM.
source: D395 forms a salt bridge to SAM and its mutation to alanine was previously shown to abolish METTL3 activity and SAM binding, confirming its involvement in cosubstrate binding (Wang et al., 2016b; Wang et al., 2016a; Śledź and Jinek, 2016).
evidence: This is shown in crystal structures and supported by citations.

claim: Mutation of D395 to alanine abolishes METTL3 activity and SAM binding.
source: D395 forms a salt bridge to SAM and its mutation to alanine was previously shown to abolish METTL3 activity and SAM binding, confirming its involvement in cosubstrate binding (Wang et al., 2016b; Wang et al., 2016a; Śledź and Jinek, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Wang et al., 2016b; Wang et al., 2016a; Śledź and Jinek, 2016 and confirmed by data in Figure 4C.

claim: There can be a hydrogen bond formed between D395 and the N6-atom of adenosine in the case of the non-alkylated RNA substrate.
source: The METTL3-BA2 structure reveals that there can also be a hydrogen bond formed between D395 and the N6-atom of adenosine in the case of the non-alkylated RNA substrate (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is shown in the crystal structure with BA2 in Figure 4.

claim: P396 in the 395DPPW398 motif, through its carbonyl group, forms a hydrogen bond to the N6-atom of adenosine.
source: P396 in the 395DPPW398 motif, through its carbonyl group, forms a hydrogen bond to the N6-atom of adenosine.
evidence: This is shown in the crystal structure with BA2.

claim: P397 from the 395DPPW398 motif makes hydrophobic contacts with SAM.
source: In addition, P397 from the 395DPPW398 motif makes hydrophobic contacts with SAM.
evidence: This is shown in the crystal structures.

claim: Adenosine is stabilised by hydrogen bonds from its N7- and O2'-atoms to the METTL3 side chains of E481 and K513, respectively.
source: The BA2 structure further shows that adenosine is stabilised by additional hydrogen bonds from its N7- and O2'-atoms to the METTL3 side chains of E481 and K513, respectively.
evidence: This is shown in the crystal structure with BA2 in Figure 4.

claim: W398 backbone carbonyl group forms a water-bridged hydrogen bond with the Y406 side chain in the BA4 structure.
source: W398 from the 395DPPW398 motif is not directly involved in adenosine binding, its backbone carbonyl group forms a water-bridged hydrogen bond with the Y406 side chain in the BA4 structure.
evidence: This is shown in the crystal structure with BA4.

claim: Y406 is involved in hydrophobic interactions with adenosine in the BA4 structure.
source: The latter is involved in hydrophobic interactions with adenosine in the BA4 structure whereas it remains flexible in the BA2-bound METTL3 structure (see Figure 4A).
evidence: This is shown in the crystal structure with BA4 in Figure 4A.

claim: Y406 remains flexible in the BA2-bound METTL3 structure.
source: The latter is involved in hydrophobic interactions with adenosine in the BA4 structure whereas it remains flexible in the BA2-bound METTL3 structure (see Figure 4A).
evidence: This is shown in the crystal structure with BA2 in Figure 4A where there is no electron density for Y406.

claim: Alanine mutation of D395, Y406, E481, and K513 almost completely abolishes the METTL3 catalytic activity.
source: Alanine mutation of D395, Y406, E481, and K513, which are involved in adenosine binding as seen in the BA2 and BA4 structures, almost completely abolishes the METTL3 catalytic activity (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is shown experimentally in Figure 4C.

claim: D395, Y406, E481, and K513 are highly conserved in METTL3.
source: Importantly, these residues are highly conserved in METTL3 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in the conservation analysis in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The loss of activity of the Y406, E481, and K513 mutants originates mainly from abolished binding capability to adenosine and not SAM.
source: The loss of activity of the Y406, E481, and K513 mutants originates mainly from abolished binding capability to adenosine and not SAM, because they can still bind SAH, as seen from a thermal shift assay (TSA) (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is shown in the thermal shift assay data in Figure 4D.

claim: Upon binding SAH, the thermal shift for the Y406, E481, and K513 mutants is similar as for the wild-type.
source: Upon binding SAH, the thermal shift for the Y406, E481, and K513 mutants is similar as for the wild-type (WT) which suggests that their side chains are not involved in binding SAM/SAH but rather the RNA substrate.
evidence: This is shown in the thermal shift assay data in Figure 4D.

claim: Mutation of D395 impairs SAH binding.
source: In contrast, mutation of D395 impairs SAH binding, which is consistent with the involvement of the D395 side chain in SAM binding (Wang et al., 2016b).
evidence: This is shown in the thermal shift assay data in Figure 4D and supported by citation.

claim: Simulations that were started with AMP or m6AMP in the conformation of BA4 showed immediate dissociation of these ligands.
source: Simulations that were started with AMP or m6AMP in the conformation of BA4 showed immediate dissociation of these ligands (see Table 2 and Figure 4—figure supplements 3 and 4).
evidence: This is shown in the MD simulation data in Table 2 and Figure 4—figure supplements 3 and 4.

claim: The BA4 conformation represents a short-lived intermediate during substrate binding or product release.
source: This could mean that this conformation represents a short-lived intermediate during substrate binding or product release.
evidence: This is inferred from the MD simulation results showing rapid dissociation from the BA4 conformation.

claim: The BA4 conformation possibly represents an encounter complex between the METTL3-SAM holo complex and RNA substrate.
source: Possibly, it represents an encounter complex between the METTL3-SAM holo complex and RNA substrate.
evidence: This is speculated based on the structural features and MD simulation results.

claim: Binding of AMP is more stable than m6AMP in the BA2 conformation.
source: Binding of AMP is more stable, while the methylated product dissociates more quickly (see Table 2).
evidence: This is shown in the MD simulation data in Table 2.

claim: The difference in binding stability between AMP and m6AMP originates, at least in part, from the long-range monopole-monopole electrostatic interaction between the positively charged SAM and the negatively charged AMP.
source: This difference originates, at least in part, from the long-range monopole-monopole electrostatic interaction between the positively charged SAM and the negatively charged AMP.
evidence: This is inferred from the MD simulation results and electrostatic considerations.

claim: After the methyl transfer reaction, SAH is neutral which does not favour interaction with m6AMP resulting in rapid dissociation of the latter.
source: After the methyl transfer reaction, SAH is neutral which does not favour interaction with m6AMP resulting in rapid dissociation of the latter.
evidence: This is inferred from the MD simulation results and electrostatic considerations.

claim: The dissociation constants of AMP and m6AMP are ~2 and ~78 mM, respectively, based on MD simulations.
source: Based on the mean lifetimes determined from the MD simulations, and assuming diffusion-limited association rates of 109 M–1s–1, the dissociation constants of AMP and m6AMP are ~2 and ~78 mM, respectively.
evidence: This is calculated from the MD simulation data assuming diffusion-limited association rates.

claim: The long GGACU motif containing mRNA can interact with the binding groove at the METTL3-14 interface with dissociation constants in the nanomolar range.
source: In contrast to these low affinities, the long GGACU motif containing mRNA can interact with the binding groove at the METTL3-14 interface with dissociation constants in the nanomolar range, resulting in a more stable complex (Qi et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Qi et al., 2022.

claim: AMP can transiently populate a binding mode similar to BA4 when starting from the BA2 conformation.
source: Nevertheless, our model is useful as it emphasises the differences in binding affinity due to the different electrostatic interactions between the SAM-AMP and SAH-m6AMP pairs. Besides the structural stability of the BA2-like pose of AMP, the MD simulations also suggest that AMP can transiently populate a binding mode similar to BA4 (Figure 4—figure supplement 7).
evidence: This is shown in the MD simulation data in Figure 4—figure supplement 7.

claim: The crystal structure of the complex with BA2 reveals a string of ionic interactions which involves charged side chains of METTL3 and the amino and carboxyl groups of the SAM analogue.
source: The crystal structure of the complex with BA2 reveals a string of ionic interactions which involves charged side chains of METTL3 and the amino and carboxyl groups of the SAM analogue.
evidence: This is shown in the crystal structure with BA2.

claim: The string of ionic interactions consists of seven charged groups: R536+ – SAM COO- – SAM NH3+ – D395- – K513+ – E481- – K459+.
source: The string consists of seven charged groups (four of which are positive): R536+ – SAM COO- – SAM NH3+ – D395- – K513+ – E481- – K459+ (see Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This is shown in the crystal structure with BA2 in Figure 4.

claim: In the BA2 conformation, the polar interactions between AMP and the charged side chains D395 and K513 are stronger than the interaction between E481 and the 2' hydroxyl group of the ribose.
source: In the BA2 conformation, the polar interactions between AMP and the charged side chains D395 and K513 are stronger than the interaction between E481 and the 2' hydroxyl group of the ribose (see Figure 4—figure supplement 5, black traces).
evidence: This is shown in the MD simulation data in Figure 4—figure supplement 5.

claim: For SAM, the interaction between its positively charged amine and D395 is more stable than the one between its negatively charged carboxy with R536.
source: For SAM, the interaction between its positively charged amine and D395 is more stable than the one between its negatively charged carboxy with R536 which can adopt different conformations (see Figure 4—figure supplement 5, blue traces).
evidence: This is shown in the MD simulation data in Figure 4—figure supplement 5.

claim: The salt bridge D395- – K513+ is the most stable intramolecular salt bridge.
source: The salt bridge D395- – K513+ seems to be the most stable, while E481- – K459+ seems to change frequently between direct and water-separated contacts.
evidence: This is shown in the MD simulation data.

claim: The D395- – K513+ salt bridge is not present in the initial apo structure but is formed during the course of the simulation.
source: In METTL3 apo trajectories, the D395- – K513+ salt bridge is not present in the initial structure but is formed during the course of the simulation (Figure 4—figure supplement 8).
evidence: This is shown in the MD simulation data in Figure 4—figure supplement 8.

claim: Y406 has been found in different conformations in structures of METTL3-14 in the apo state or bound to SAH or SAM.
source: In structures of METTL3-14 in the apo state or bound to SAH or SAM, METTL3 residue Y406 is found in different conformations (Wang et al., 2016b; Wang et al., 2016a; Śledź and Jinek, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Wang et al., 2016b; Wang et al., 2016a; Śledź and Jinek, 2016.

claim: One study suggested that Y406 makes a hydrogen bond with S511 in ASL2 and thereby caps the SAH coproduct.
source: One study suggested that Y406 makes a hydrogen bond with S511 in ASL2 and thereby caps the SAH coproduct (Śledź and Jinek, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Śledź and Jinek, 2016.

claim: Another study suggested that Y406 might be important for the interaction with nucleotide bases.
source: However, another study suggested that Y406 might be important for the interaction with nucleotide bases (Wang et al., 2016a).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wang et al., 2016a.

claim: The different conformations of Y406 seen in the crystal structures with BA2 and BA4 suggest an involvement of the Y406 side chain in RNA nucleotide binding, probably as a first step of RNA recognition.
source: The different conformations of Y406 seen in our crystal structures with BA2 and BA4 support the latter and suggest an involvement of the Y406 side chain in RNA nucleotide binding, probably as a first step of RNA recognition (see Figure 4A).
evidence: This is inferred from the crystal structures shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Mutation of Y406 to alanine or cysteine abolishes MTase activity.
source: Indeed, mutation of Y406 to alanine (in this and a previous study) or cysteine (in a previous study) abolishes MTase activity (see Figure 4C; Wang et al., 2016a; Śledź and Jinek, 2016).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4C and supported by citations to Wang et al., 2016a; Śledź and Jinek, 2016.

claim: Y406 transitions multiple times on the µs time scale from orientations far away from the W398 carbonyl oxygen to shorter distances.
source: In the MD simulations, Y406 transitions multiple times (on the µs time scale) from orientations far away from the W398 carbonyl oxygen (distance of ~15 Å) to shorter distances of ~6 Å (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is shown in the MD simulation data in Figure 5A.

claim: The adenine ring system of AMP can be involved in a π-π interaction with Y406 for several ns before exiting the pocket.
source: We observe that the adenine ring system of AMP can be involved in a π-π interaction with Y406 for several ns before exiting the pocket, and is then captured again later by the Y406 side chain, but is not brought back into the pocket (Figure 5—video 1).
evidence: This is shown in the MD simulation data and video.

claim: In the METTL3 SAM-bound state, the Y406 side chain is flexible.
source: In the METTL3 SAM-bound state, the Y406 side chain is flexible.
evidence: This is inferred from the MD simulation data.

claim: To bind RNA effectively, Y406 needs to stabilise through the water-bridged polar interaction with the backbone of W398.
source: To bind RNA effectively, Y406 needs to stabilise through the water-bridged polar interaction with the backbone of W398.
evidence: This is inferred from the crystal structures and MD simulations.

claim: Y406 plays a role in positioning the adenosine substrate at the catalytic site.
source: Additionally, Y406 plays a role in positioning the adenosine substrate at the catalytic site.
evidence: This is inferred from the crystal structures and MD simulations.

claim: The cosubstrate SAM is expected to bind before the RNA substrate given the high concentration of SAM in the cell.
source: Given the high concentration of SAM in the cell (60–160 μM in the rat liver), the cosubstrate SAM is expected to bind before the RNA substrate (Finkelstein and Martin, 1984).
evidence: This is inferred from the high cellular concentration of SAM cited from Finkelstein and Martin, 1984.

claim: SAM binding results in large conformational changes of several side chains in the METTL3 active site.
source: SAM binding results in large conformational changes of several side chains in the METTL3 active site (Figure 6).
evidence: This is shown in the structural comparison in Figure 6.

claim: In the apo state, the K513 side chain points away from the putative RNA binding site and is involved in intramolecular polar contacts with the side chains of Y518, E532, and, via a water molecule, D395.
source: In the apo state, the K513 side chain points away from the putative RNA binding site and is involved in intramolecular polar contacts with the side chains of Y518, E532, and, via a water molecule, D395, that probably help to stabilise the apo protein (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is shown in the structural comparison in Figure 6A.

claim: SAM binding disrupts the water-mediated hydrogen bond between K513 and D395.
source: SAM binding disrupts the water-mediated hydrogen bond between K513 and D395.
evidence: This is shown in the structural comparison in Figure 6.

claim: SAM binding leads to a conformational change in the K513 side chain which then points in the direction of the RNA binding site where it can form a direct salt bridge with D395.
source: This leads to a conformational change in the K513 side chain which then points in the direction of the RNA binding site where it can form a direct salt bridge with D395.
evidence: This is shown in the structural comparison in Figure 6.

claim: In the SAM-bound conformation, the K513 side chain can readily form a hydrogen bond to the adenosine-N7 of an RNA substrate as seen in the BA2 structure.
source: In that conformation, the K513 side chain can also readily form a hydrogen bond to the adenosine-N7 of an RNA substrate as seen in the BA2 structure (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is shown in the crystal structure with BA2 in Figure 6B.

claim: The side chain of H512 undergoes a conformational change upon SAM binding.
source: Furthermore, the side chain of H512, which is part of the SAM binding pocket environment, also undergoes a conformational change upon SAM binding (see Figure 6A).
evidence: This is shown in the structural comparison in Figure 6A.

claim: In the apo state, the H512 side chain points inwards and thus blocks the adenosine binding site.
source: In the apo state, the H512 side chain points inwards and thus blocks the adenosine binding site.
evidence: This is shown in the structural comparison in Figure 6.

claim: Once SAM is bound, the H512 side chain is attracted to form a π-π interaction with H538.
source: However, once SAM is bound, the H512 side chain is attracted to form a π-π interaction with H538 whose side chain rotates from an outward pointing conformation in the apo state to an inward pointing conformation in which it interacts with SAM in the holo state.
evidence: This is shown in the structural comparison in Figure 6.

claim: The conformational change of the H512 side chain makes space for adenosine to bind as seen in the BA2 structure.
source: This conformational change of the H512 side chain makes space for adenosine to bind as seen in the BA2 structure (see Figure 6B).
evidence: This is shown in the crystal structure with BA2 in Figure 6B.

claim: The side chains of both H512 and K513 are flexible in the apo state, but undergo stabilisation upon SAM and adenosine binding.
source: MD simulations show that the side chains of both H512 and K513 are flexible in the apo state, but undergo stabilisation upon SAM and adenosine binding (Figure 4—figure supplements 5 and 8 and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in the MD simulation data.

claim: The conformational switches of the H512 and K513 side chains upon SAM binding can be seen as priming METTL3 for adenosine binding.
source: Together, the conformational switches of the H512 and K513 side chains upon SAM binding can be seen as priming METTL3 for adenosine binding.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural changes observed upon SAM binding.

claim: When the SAM moiety of BA2 is superimposed with SAM bound to METTL4 and METTL16, the adenosine moiety of BA2 is situated in a very similar position as the substrates of the other MTases.
source: When the SAM moiety of BA2 is superimposed with SAM bound to METTL4 and METTL16, the adenosine moiety of BA2 is situated in a very similar position as the substrates of the other MTases (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is shown in the structural comparison in Figure 7A.

claim: In METTL4, the N6-atom of substrate adenosine is positioned at a distance of 2.8 Å from the methyl group of SAM.
source: In METTL4 and METTL16, the N6-atom of their substrate adenosine (analogue) is positioned at a distance of 2.8 and 2.1 Å from the methyl group of SAM, respectively (Figure 7B and C).
evidence: This is shown in the structural comparison in Figure 7B.

claim: In METTL16, the N6-atom of substrate adenosine is positioned at a distance of 2.1 Å from the methyl group of SAM.
source: In METTL4 and METTL16, the N6-atom of their substrate adenosine (analogue) is positioned at a distance of 2.8 and 2.1 Å from the methyl group of SAM, respectively (Figure 7B and C).
evidence: This is shown in the structural comparison in Figure 7C.

claim: The angle formed between SAM-5'S – Cε – adenosine-N6 in the substrate-cosubstrate pairs of METTL4 is 162.5°.
source: The angle formed between SAM-5'S – Cε – adenosine-N6 in the substrate-cosubstrate pairs of METTL4 and METTL16 is 162.5° and 175.4°, respectively.
evidence: This is measured from the structural comparison in Figure 7B.

claim: The angle formed between SAM-5'S – Cε – adenosine-N6 in the substrate-cosubstrate pairs of METTL16 is 175.4°.
source: The angle formed between SAM-5'S – Cε – adenosine-N6 in the substrate-cosubstrate pairs of METTL4 and METTL16 is 162.5° and 175.4°, respectively.
evidence: This is measured from the structural comparison in Figure 7C.

claim: In BA2, the adenosine-N6 is situated at 1.9 Å away from the carbon corresponding to the Cε-atom of the methionine moiety in the SAM cofactor.
source: In BA2, the adenosine-N6 is situated, through the alkyl chain of the linker, at 1.9 Å away from the carbon corresponding to the Cε-atom of the methionine moiety in the SAM cofactor (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is measured from the crystal structure with BA2 shown in Figure 7D.

claim: The 1.9 Å distance in the crystal structure with BA2 is similar to the corresponding distance in METTL4 and METTL16, which would allow for an SN2 transfer of the methyl group.
source: The 1.9 Å distance in the crystal structure with BA2 is similar to the corresponding distance in METTL4 and METTL16, which, in two non-linked moieties, would allow for an SN2 transfer of the methyl group of a METTL3-bound SAM to the N6-atom of an adenosine substrate.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing the distances in the different structures.

claim: The angle formed by the SAM-5'S – Cε – adenosine-N6 in METTL3 is 160.9°.
source: Strikingly, the angle formed by the SAM-5'S – Cε – adenosine-N6 in METTL3 is 160.9° which is similar to the other MTases, and very close to the optimal 180° for an SN2 reaction in which the adenosine-N6 attacks the SAM-Cε and SAH becomes the leaving group.
evidence: This is measured from the crystal structure with BA2.

claim: The angle of 160.9° in METTL3 is very close to the optimal 180° for an SN2 reaction.
source: Strikingly, the angle formed by the SAM-5'S – Cε – adenosine-N6 in METTL3 is 160.9° which is similar to the other MTases, and very close to the optimal 180° for an SN2 reaction in which the adenosine-N6 attacks the SAM-Cε and SAH becomes the leaving group.
evidence: This is based on chemical knowledge of SN2 reactions.

claim: The adenosine of BA2 is in a suitable orientation for methyl transfer.
source: Hence, the adenosine of BA2 is in a suitable orientation for methyl transfer and BA2 represents a transition state mimic for METTL3.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural analysis showing the appropriate distance and angle for SN2 reaction.

claim: BA2 represents a transition state mimic for METTL3.
source: Hence, the adenosine of BA2 is in a suitable orientation for methyl transfer and BA2 represents a transition state mimic for METTL3.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural analysis showing the appropriate distance and angle for SN2 reaction.

claim: The methyl transfer mechanism in METTL3 has a free energy barrier of 15–16 kcal/mol.
source: Indeed, third-order density functional tight binding (DFTB3)/MM free energy simulations show that this mechanism is energetically favourable (by about ~4 kcal/mol) with a barrier of 15–16 kcal/mol (Figure 8B and Figure 8—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: This is calculated from QM/MM free energy simulations shown in Figure 8B.

claim: The methyl transfer mechanism in METTL3 is energetically favourable by about ~4 kcal/mol.
source: Indeed, third-order density functional tight binding (DFTB3)/MM free energy simulations show that this mechanism is energetically favourable (by about ~4 kcal/mol) with a barrier of 15–16 kcal/mol (Figure 8B and Figure 8—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: This is calculated from QM/MM free energy simulations shown in Figure 8B.

claim: The catalytic turnover of METTL3-14 is 0.2–0.6 min–1 at ambient temperature which implies a barrier of ~20 kcal/mol.
source: The catalytic turnover of METTL3-14, as measured by an enzymatic RNA methylation assay, is 0.2–0.6 min–1 at ambient temperature which implies a barrier of ~20 kcal/mol (Buker et al., 2020; Garcia-Viloca et al., 2004; Glowacki et al., 2012).
evidence: This is based on experimental measurements cited from Buker et al., 2020 and transition state theory.

claim: The methyl transfer is not the rate-limiting step in METTL3 catalysis.
source: Hence, the methyl transfer is not the rate-limiting step.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing the QM/MM barrier (15-16 kcal/mol) with the experimental barrier (~20 kcal/mol).

claim: The reaction in the enzyme is substantially more exoergic compared to the model reaction in solution.
source: Compared to the model reaction in solution computed using a continuum solvation model (Table 3), the reaction in the enzyme is substantially more exoergic, suggesting that the enzyme environment stabilises the product of the methyl transfer reaction.
evidence: This is shown by comparing the QM/MM results with gas-phase and solution calculations in Table 3.

claim: The enzyme environment stabilises the product of the methyl transfer reaction.
source: Compared to the model reaction in solution computed using a continuum solvation model (Table 3), the reaction in the enzyme is substantially more exoergic, suggesting that the enzyme environment stabilises the product of the methyl transfer reaction.
evidence: This is inferred from the QM/MM calculations showing more favorable energetics in the enzyme.

claim: Product stabilisation primarily comes from the hydrogen-bonding interactions between the adenosine-N6 group and nearby polar groups, in particular the side chain of D395 and the backbone carbonyl of P396.
source: Inspection of the active site structure based on DFTB3/MM simulations suggests that such stabilisation primarily comes from the hydrogen-bonding interactions between the adenosine-N6 group and nearby polar groups, in particular the side chain of D395 and the backbone carbonyl of P396 (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is shown in the QM/MM simulation snapshots in Figure 8C.

claim: This catalytic mechanism is similar to N6-adenine DNA methyl transferase M·TaqI.
source: This catalytic mechanism is similar to N6-adenine DNA methyl transferase M·TaqI, in which the adenosine-N6 group is hydrogen-bonded to an Asn side chain and backbone carbonyl of a Pro in the protein (Goedecke et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Goedecke et al., 2001.

claim: In M·TaqI, it was proposed that the methyl transfer occurs first, leading to an adenine-m6NH2+ group well stabilised by hydrogen-bonding interactions.
source: In the absence of any catalytic base, it was proposed that the methyl transfer occurs first, leading to an adenine-m6NH2+ group well stabilised by hydrogen-bonding interactions with the Asn side chain and Pro backbone carbonyl.
evidence: This is based on the mechanism proposed for M·TaqI.

claim: The M·TaqI mechanism was supported by QM/MM free energy simulations with a barrier height of ~20 kcal/mol.
source: The mechanism was supported by QM/MM free energy simulations with a barrier height of ~20 kcal/mol (Aranda et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Aranda et al., 2014.

claim: When the active site Asn in M·TaqI was replaced by an Asp, a mechanism in which deprotonation of the adenine-N6 group by the Asp preceded the methyl transfer also had a comparable free energy barrier.
source: On the other hand, the same QM/MM study suggested that when the active site Asn was replaced by an Asp, a mechanism in which deprotonation of the adenine-N6 group by the Asp preceded the methyl transfer from SAM also had a comparable free energy barrier.
evidence: This is based on QM/MM studies of M·TaqI variants.

claim: DNA N6-methyltransferases in the α/β groups feature an Asp in the active site, while those in the γ group have an Asn at the equivalent position.
source: DNA N6-methyltransferases in the α/β groups feature an Asp in the active site, while those in the γ group have an Asn at the equivalent position (Malone et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Malone et al., 1995.

claim: The adenosine-N6 position has a very high pKa of ~17.
source: The adenosine-N6 position has a very high pKa of ~17, and thus its deprotonation requires a particularly strong base, which is absent in the active site of METTL3-14.
evidence: This is based on chemical knowledge and supported by citation to Lippert, 2005.

claim: Deprotonation of adenosine-N6 requires a particularly strong base, which is absent in the active site of METTL3-14.
source: The adenosine-N6 position has a very high pKa of ~17, and thus its deprotonation requires a particularly strong base, which is absent in the active site of METTL3-14.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural features of the METTL3 active site.

claim: D395 forms a salt bridge with K513 and therefore is expected to feature a too low pKa value to deprotonate the adenosine-N6H2.
source: For example, while there is a carboxylate nearby (D395), it forms a salt bridge with K513, and therefore is expected to feature a too low pKa value to deprotonate the adenosine-N6H2.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural features and electrostatic considerations.

claim: The computed DFTB3/MM free energy profile without adenosine-N6 deprotonation is consistent with the reported experimental kinetics.
source: These considerations are congruent with the observation that the computed DFTB3/MM free energy profile without adenosine-N6 deprotonation is possible within the reported experimental kinetics (Buker et al., 2020; Woodcock et al., 2019; Xiao et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by comparing the QM/MM results with experimental data cited from Buker et al., 2020; Woodcock et al., 2019; Xiao et al., 2022.

claim: Adenosine-N6 becomes much more acidic following methylation.
source: The difference in the methylation energetics of adenosine in different protonation states shown in Table 3 is consistent with the pKa difference of adenosine before and after methylation. Thus, the large difference suggests that adenosine-N6 becomes much more acidic following methylation, which is consistent with literature estimates of the pKa values of N6-protonated adenosine derivatives in the range of –3 to –10 (Kettani et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by the calculations in Table 3 and citation to Kettani et al., 1997.

claim: The pKa values of N6-protonated adenosine derivatives are in the range of –3 to –10.
source: Thus, the large difference suggests that adenosine-N6 becomes much more acidic following methylation, which is consistent with literature estimates of the pKa values of N6-protonated adenosine derivatives in the range of –3 to –10 (Kettani et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kettani et al., 1997.

claim: The proton release following methylation may occur readily through water wires that connect the adenosine-N6 position to the protein-solvent interface.
source: Close inspection of the active site structure in the product state of DFTB3/MM simulations reveals that the proton release may occur readily through water wires that connect the adenosine-N6 position to the protein-solvent interface (Figure 9).
evidence: This is shown in the QM/MM simulation snapshot in Figure 9.

claim: Favourable salt bridges in the active site do not have to break to allow the proton release following methylation of the substrate.
source: Therefore, favourable salt bridges in the active site (e.g. D395-K513) do not have to break to allow the proton release following methylation of the substrate.
evidence: This is inferred from the presence of water channels for proton release shown in Figure 9.

claim: METTL4 belongs to a subclade of MT-A70 family members of MTases.
source: Finally, we note that the recently solved crystal structures of METTL4, which belongs to a subclade of MT-A70 family members of MTases, showed an active site very similar to that of METTL3 (Luo et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Luo et al., 2022.

claim: METTL4 has an active site very similar to that of METTL3.
source: Finally, we note that the recently solved crystal structures of METTL4, which belongs to a subclade of MT-A70 family members of MTases, showed an active site very similar to that of METTL3 (Luo et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Luo et al., 2022.

source: A nearby ion pair (D233-K364) is engaged in a hydrogen-bonding network involving both the substrate and SAM.
evidence: This is based on the structural similarity between METTL4 and METTL3.

claim: The catalytic mechanism discussed for METTL3 applies also to METTL4 and potentially other MT-A70 family members of MTases.
source: Therefore, we expect that the catalytic mechanism discussed here applies also to METTL4 and potentially other MT-A70 family members of MTases.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural similarity between METTL3 and METTL4.
